messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Source: Piezoelectric energy harvester (current source $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and $20\text{ M}\Omega$).
    *   Goal: Power $R_L$ from $C_{out}$ at node `out`.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
    *   Challenges:
        *   $V_{oc}$ is low ($\approx 3.2\text{ V}$ nominal), so diode drops in a full bridge are significant (Reference Design FBR fails S2 and S4).
        *   S3 (Strong excitation, light load) causes $v_{max}$ to exceed $3.6\text{ V}$ (FBR fails S3).
        *   S4 (Weak excitation) fails $v_{avg}$ and $t_{up}$ (FBR fails S4).
        *   The ripple requirement is very tight ($50\text{ mV}$).

    *   FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier) is simple but inefficient due to diode drops.
    *   S3 shows a need for over-voltage protection (Zener clamp).
    *   S2 and S4 show a need for higher efficiency (lower voltage drop) or energy extraction enhancement.
    *   Standard energy harvesting techniques:
        *   SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor): Uses an inductor and a switch to invert the charge on $C_p$ at peaks, significantly increasing power extraction.
        *   Active Rectification: Synchronous rectification to replace diodes.
        *   Charge Pumps: To boost voltage (though $V_{oc}$ is quite low).

    *   *Proposal 1: SSHI (Parallel-SSHI or similar).*
        *   An inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ are used to flip the polarity of $C_p$ at the peaks of the voltage.
        *   Connectivity: Piezo ($pzp, pzn$) -> Bridge $\rightarrow$ $C_{out}$. Switch $S$ and inductor $L$ in parallel with the piezo (or in a specific configuration).
        *   Let's try a basic SSHI-like structure: a bridge to rectify, but an inductor and switch to "flip" the voltage.
        *   Actually, a simpler high-efficiency approach for low $V_{oc}$ is an inductor-based buck-boost or a synchronous rectifier. But since we have a `SYNC` controller, we can implement a resonant flip.

    *   *Proposal 2: Full Bridge with Zener Clamp (FBR+Zener).*
        *   Fixes the $v_{max}$ issue in S3.
        *   Still might fail S2 and S4 due to diode drops.
        *   Wait, the goal is to meet *every* condition. FBR failed S2, S3, S4. Zener only fixes S3.

    *   *Proposal 3: Synchronous Rectifier (using SYNC switches).*
        *   Replace diodes with switches controlled by `SYNC`.
        *   `S1` and `S2` switches for the bridge.
        *   Since we only have 2 `SYNC` controllers and 4 switches max, we can't do a full active bridge easily.
        *   Half-bridge or a specific SSHI topology.

    *   *Refining Proposal 1 (SSHI-ish):*
        *   Use an inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ to invert the piezo voltage.
        *   Circuit: Piezo terminals `pzp`, `pzn`. A switch $S$ and Inductor $L$ in series between `pzp` and `pzn`? No, that just shorts it.
        *   The classic SSHI: A switch $S$ in series with $L$ connects the piezo to a capacitor or flips the polarity.
        *   Wait, the simplest "power boost" is the "Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor" (SSHI). The switch $S$ is closed for a short time $t_{on}$ at the voltage peaks.
        *   Topology: Piezo -> Full Bridge -> $C_{out}$. Parallel to the piezo: a branch with Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$.
        *   When $S$ closes at the peak, $L$ and $C_p$ resonate, flipping the voltage on $C_p$ and pushing more charge through the bridge.
        *   This significantly increases $v_{avg}$ for S2 and S4.
        *   To handle S3 ($v_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$), add a Zener diode $DZ33$.

    *   *Refining Proposal 2 (Active Rectifier / Sync Switch):*
        *   Instead of a bridge, use a switch and a diode.
        *   Actually, let's look at the `SYNC` controller specs. It triggers at extrema.
        *   A simple "Synchronous" approach: Use `S` to connect the piezo to `out` only when the piezo voltage is higher than `out`.
        *   Since we have 2 `SYNC` controllers, we can do a "half-bridge" or two-switch system.

    *   *Let's go with a high-performance SSHI variant:*
        *   Components:
            1.  Full Bridge (4 x DSCH)
            2.  Storage Capacitor (Cout)
            3.  Zener Clamp (DZ33) to protect $v_{max}$.
            4.  SSHI circuit: Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo terminals `pzp`, `pzn`.
            5.  `SYNC` controller to trigger the switch $S$ at both peaks.

    *   *Wait, will the SSHI branch increase $v_{max}$ too much?*
        *   Yes, that's why the Zener is critical.

    *   *Let's double-check the SSHI topology:*
        *   Piezo: `pzp`, `pzn`.
        *   Bridge: `D1(pzp, out)`, `D2(pzn, out)`, `D3(0, pzp)`, `D4(0, pzn)`. (Wait, return diodes: `D3` anode at 0, cathode at `pzp`; `D4` anode at 0, cathode at `pzn`).
        *   SSHI: `L1` between `pzp` and `n1`, `S1` between `n1` and `pzn`.
        *   `SYNC` G1: `edges: both`, `ton` ~ $\pi\sqrt{L C_p}$.

    *   *Alternative: The "Synchronous" rectifier approach (Active bridge)*
        *   With only 4 switches, we could replace 2 diodes of the bridge.
        *   But the SSHI is much more powerful for low $V_{oc}$.

    *   *Evaluating the FBR+SSHI+Zener:*
        *   $v_{avg}$ increase: SSHI boosts the effective voltage, helping S2 and S4.
        *   $v_{max}$ control: DZ33 clamps it at 3.3V, helping S3.
        *   $v_{pp}$ control: Large $C_{out}$ and Zener help.
        *   $t_{up}$ control: SSHI speeds up charging.

    *   *Let's consider a second topology just in case: a simpler Charge Pump or a different SSHI variant.*
        *   Maybe a "Parallel-SSHI"?
        *   Actually, let's try:
            1. SSHI + FBR + Zener.
            2. Synchronous Half-Bridge (S1, S2 instead of diodes) + Zener.
            3. FBR + Zener (as a baseline to see if Zener alone is enough, but FBR already failed S2/S4).

    *   *Refining Topology 1: SSHI-FBR-Zener*
        *   `D1`: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`
        *   `D2`: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out`
        *   `D3`: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp`
        *   `D4`: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzn`
        *   `Cout`: `out` $\rightarrow$ `0`
        *   `DZ1`: `0` $\rightarrow$ `out` (Zener, cathode on `out`)
        *   `L1`: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `n1`
        *   `S1`: `n1` $\rightarrow$ `pzn`
        *   `G1`: `SYNC` (edges: both, ton: 30us)

    *   *Refining Topology 2: SSHI-FBR (No Zener, but maybe a resistive divider or different C? No, Zener is the way).*
        *   Let's try a different SSHI: "Series SSHI".
        *   Series SSHI uses a capacitor to block DC and a switch to flip. It's more complex.
        *   Let's stick to the Parallel SSHI but maybe use a different bridge.

    *   *Refining Topology 3: Synchronous rectification using switches for the main path.*
        *   If we use switches `S1` and `S2` to connect `pzp` and `pzn` to `out` respectively, we eliminate diode drops.
        *   `S1` (ctrl G1, edges: pos): `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`
        *   `S2` (ctrl G2, edges: neg): `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out`
        *   This is a "synchronous half-bridge". We still need a way to handle the negative swing of the piezo relative to ground.
        *   Wait, if we only connect to `out` during the positive peak, we only get half the energy.
        *   To get both halves, we'd need a full active bridge (4 switches). We have 4 switches!
        *   Active Bridge:
            *   `S1`: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out` (G1, pos)
            *   `S2`: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out` (G2, neg)
            *   `S3`: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp` (G1, neg)
            *   `S4`: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzn` (G2, pos)
            *   Wait, G1 and G2 are just timers.
            *   `G1`: `edges: both`. `S1` closes at peak, `S3` closes at trough? No, the `SYNC` triggers at extrema.
            *   Actually, the `S` controller is simple: "closes its switches for `ton` seconds at the piezo voltage extrema".
            *   If `G1` is `edges: both`, `S1` and `S3` both close at the same time. That doesn't work.

    *   *Back to SSHI + FBR + Zener.* It's a robust, well-known topology for this problem.
    *   Let's try to optimize the components in the JSON.
    *   $L = 10\text{ mH}$, $C_{out} = 10\text{ uF}$ (for ripple), $t_{on} = \pi\sqrt{L C_p} = 3.14 \cdot \sqrt{0.01 \cdot 25\cdot 10^{-9}} \approx 15.7\text{ uS}$.

    *   S1: Nominal (FBR worked $v_{avg}$, $v_{max}$ etc.)
    *   S2: Heavy load (FBR failed $v_{avg} \rightarrow 1.76\text{ V}$). SSHI will boost this.
    *   S3: Strong excitation (FBR failed $v_{max} \rightarrow 5.72\text{ V}$). DZ33 will clamp this to $\approx 3.3\text{ V}$.
    *   S4: Weak excitation (FBR failed $v_{avg} \rightarrow 1.51\text{ V}$). SSHI will boost this.
    *   S5: Low frequency (FBR failed settled $dv$). Higher $C_{out}$ should help.
    *   S6: Hot/Cap change (FBR worked).

    *   Wait, I can provide up to 3 designs. Let's provide a few variations of the SSHI and maybe one active approach.
    *   Design 1: SSHI + FBR + Zener (The most promising).
    *   Design 2: SSHI + FBR (No Zener, to see if the evolution strategy can find a way with $C_{out}$ or just to have a baseline). Actually, better to provide something different.
    *   Design 3: A simplified synchronous rectifier: `S1` (`pzp` to `out`, `G1` pos), `S2` (`pzn` to `out`, `G2` neg) and two diodes `D1` (`0` to `pzp`), `D2` (`0` to `pzn`). This reduces diode drops on the high-current path.

    *   `D1`: `pzp`, `out` (DSCH)
    *   `D2`: `pzn`, `out` (DSCH)
    *   `D3`: `0`, `pzp` (DSCH)
    *   `D4`: `0`, `pzn` (DSCH)
    *   `C1`: `out`, `0` (Value: $10\text{ uF}$)
    *   `DZ1`: `0`, `out` (DZ33)
    *   `L1`: `pzp`, `n1` (Value: $10\text{ mH}$)
    *   `S1`: `n1`, `pzn` (Ctrl: `G1`)
    *   `G1`: `SYNC` (`ton`: $15\text{ uS}$, `edges`: `both`, `phase`: $0$)

    *   Is $10\text{ uF}$ within range? Yes (max $47\text{ uF}$).
    *   Is $10\text{ mH}$ within range? Yes (max $10\text{ mH}$).
    *   Is `DSCH` the best diode? Yes.
    *   Is the Zener `DZ33` correctly oriented? Yes, `["0", "out"]` (cathode on `out`).
    *   Is the SSHI connection correct? Yes, `L1` and `S1` in series across the piezo.
    *   Number of components: 4 diodes + 1 cap + 1 zener + 1 inductor + 1 switch + 1 sync = 9 components (under the limit of 16).

    *   S2/S4: $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$? SSHI generally increases harvested power by $2\text{--}5\text{x}$. FBR was at $1.5\text{--}1.7\text{ V}$, so SSHI should easily push it over $1.8\text{ V}$.
    *   S3: $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$? DZ33 clamps at $3.3\text{ V}$.
    *   Ripple: $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$? $10\text{ uF}$ is quite large; should be fine.
    *   Startup: $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$? SSHI accelerates charging.
    *   Settled: $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$? Large $C_{out}$ helps stability.

    *   Wait, let's check the `SYNC` controller `ton` again. For SSHI, the optimal $t_{on}$ is roughly the time for a quarter-cycle of the $L-C_p$ resonance: $t_{on} = \frac{\pi}{2} \sqrt{L C_p}$.
    *   $\frac{\pi}{2} \sqrt{10\text{ mH} \cdot 25\text{ nF}} = 1.57 \cdot \sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-7}} \approx 1.57 \cdot 5 \cdot 10^{-4} \approx 7.8\text{ uS}$.
    *   I'll propose $15\text{ uS}$ as a starting point, and the optimizer will tune it.

    *   `D1`: `["pzp", "out"]`
    *   `D2`: `["pzn", "out"]`
    *   `D3`: `["0", "pzp"]`
    *   `D4`: `["0", "pzn"]`
    *   `C1`: `["out", "0"]`
    *   `DZ1`: `["0", "out"]`
    *   `L1`: `["pzp", "n1"]`
    *   `S1`: `["n1", "pzn"]`
    *   `G1`: `SYNC`

    Wait, should the SSHI switch be in parallel with the piezo *before* the bridge? Yes, that's the standard Parallel-SSHI. The inductor and switch are in parallel with the piezo.

    *Wait*, if I put the SSHI in parallel with the piezo, the current during the flip will also go through the bridge. Is that okay? Yes, that's how it works. The bridge rectifies the "flipped" energy too.

    Let's consider one more design for robustness:
    Design 2: Same as Design 1, but with a smaller $L$ and larger $C_{out}$. (The optimizer handles values, but connectivity is what matters). Let's instead try a "Synchronous Half-Bridge" where we replace the two top diodes with switches.

    Design 2:
    *   `S1`: `["pzp", "out"]` (ctrl `G1`, `edges: pos`)
    *   `S2`: `["pzn", "out"]` (ctrl `G2`, `edges: neg`)
    *   `D3`: `["0", "pzp"]` (DSCH)
    *   `D4`: `["0", "pzn"]` (DSCH)
    *   `C1`: `["out", "0"]`
    *   `DZ1`: `["0", "out"]` (DZ33)
    *   This removes the drop of the top two diodes.

    Wait, the `SYNC` controller triggers at *extrema*. For `S1` to act as a rectifier, it should be closed when $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$. The piezo voltage is a sine wave. The peak is the extrema. If $t_{on}$ is very small, it only harvests at the peak. If $t_{on}$ is large, it's just a switch. This is not a standard rectifier.

    The standard rectifier diodes are better unless we have a complex controller. The `SYNC` controller provided is specifically designed for SSHI (short pulses at extrema). So the FBR+SSHI is the most appropriate use of the provided tools.

    I will propose two variations of the SSHI:
    1. FBR + SSHI + Zener (Parallel SSHI)
    2. FBR + SSHI (No Zener, just in case the Zener's leakage affects S4, though unlikely) -> Actually, let's try an SSHI where the inductor is in series with the bridge. No, that's not standard.

    Let's try:
    1. FBR + SSHI + Zener.
    2. FBR + Zener (as a check, though likely to fail S4).
    3. a version of SSHI where the switch and inductor are placed differently? No, the standard parallel is best.

    Actually, the prompt says "propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity".
    Connectivity 1: FBR + Zener + Parallel SSHI.
    Connectivity 2: FBR + Zener. (Simply the reference FBR plus a Zener clamp).
    Connectivity 3: Half-Bridge (Diodes) + Zener + Parallel SSHI (Wait, half-bridge means only one side of the piezo is rectified. Not good).

    Let's go with:
    1. Parallel SSHI + FBR + Zener.
    2. Parallel SSHI + FBR (No Zener).
    3. FBR + Zener.

    Wait, if FBR + Zener is just a variant, maybe I can try a different way to clamp. But DZ33 is the only tool.

    Let's refine the Parallel SSHI + FBR + Zener.
    Nodes: `pzp`, `pzn`, `out`, `0`, `n1`.
    Diodes: `D1(pzp, out)`, `D2(pzn, out)`, `D3(0, pzp)`, `D4(0, pzn)`.
    Cap: `C1(out, 0)`.
    Zener: `DZ1(0, out)`.
    Inductor: `L1(pzp, n1)`.
    Switch: `S1(n1, pzn)`.
    Sync: `G1(edges: both, ton: 15uS)`.

    Double-check:
    - `vavg >= 1.8V`: SSHI boosts power.
    - `vmax <= 3.6V`: DZ33 clamps at 3.3V.
    - `vpp <= 0.05V`: $C_{out}$ filters.
    - `tup <= 0.4s`: SSHI boosts charging rate.
    - `dv <= 0.02V`: Large $C_{out}$ and stability.

    Wait, does the Parallel SSHI increase $V_{max}$? Yes, it can. But the Zener will catch it.
    The most critical thing is to make sure the SSHI actually works. The `ton` and `L` must be tuned.

    One final check on the `S` switch: `S` connects `a` and `b`. `L` is in series.
    `L1`: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `n1`
    `S1`: `n1` $\rightarrow$ `pzn`
    When `S1` closes, `pzp`, `L1`, and `pzn` form a loop. This is the standard Parallel SSHI.

    Wait, the `S` component has `Ron = 2 Ohm` and `Roff = 1 GOhm`. This is perfect.

    What about the `SYNC` controller's `phase`?
    For Parallel SSHI, you want to switch at the voltage peaks. The `SYNC` triggers at "piezo voltage extrema". This is exactly what we need. `phase: 0` should be correct.

    Let's provide these three:
    1. `sshi_fbr_zener` (The main candidate)
    2. `fbr_zener` (To isolate the effect of SSHI)
    3. `sshi_fbr` (To isolate the effect of the Zener)

    Actually, the prompt says "different connectivity".
    `fbr_zener` is just `sshi_fbr_zener` without the $L$ and $S$.
    `sshi_fbr` is just `sshi_fbr_zener` without the $DZ33$.
    These are indeed different connectivities.
